summary: Defines MIB objects for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units, the Ethernet interface hardware. It obsoletes RFC 3636 and changes how MAU type identities are handled.

plainLanguage.summary:
A Medium Attachment Unit, or MAU, is the box of electronics behind an Ethernet port that turns electrical signals on the cable into data the network can carry. This RFC defines the SNMP objects that let a management system read and change the state of those units: what kind they are, whether the link works, how many times it has dropped, and what the connector looks like.

It also splits the definitions in two. The names of new cable types live in a small module that IANA updates, so a new Ethernet standard does not force a new RFC.

subtitle: The SNMP MIB for Ethernet's physical-layer attachment units, now split so new media types need no new RFC.

tldr.problem: Ethernet hardware keeps changing: new speeds, new cabling and new interfaces keep appearing, and every one of them needs to be visible to a network management system.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SNMP managed objects that describe the Medium Attachment Unit behind each Ethernet port, and splits the definitions in two: a stable MAU-MIB module and an IANA-maintained module holding the names and enumerations that change when a new medium is standardised.
tldr.outcome: A new MAU type now needs only a revised IANA module, not a new RFC, so the base MIB stays unchanged. The document obsoletes RFC 3636.

today: RFC 4836 is a Proposed Standard from April 2007. It obsoletes RFC 3636 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The document notes that its definitions reflect one stage in the evolution of Ethernet technology, and that the Ethernet Interfaces and Hub MIB Working Group may later revise or replace it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols in the Internet community. In particular, it defines objects for managing IEEE 802.3 Medium Attachment Units (MAUs).

The previous version of this document, RFC 3636, defined a single MIB module. This document splits the original MIB module into two, putting frequently updated object identities and textual conventions into a separate, IANA-maintained MIB module, in order to decrease the need of updating the basic MAU MIB module.

The first version of the IANA-maintained MIB module also extends the list of managed objects to support Ethernet in the First Mile (EFM) and 10GBASE-CX4 interfaces.

Ethernet technology continues to evolve, with scalable increases in speed, new types of cabling and interfaces, and new features. The RFC notes that this document reflects a certain stage in that evolution, and that it might later be revised, or replaced by new documents, by the Ethernet Interfaces and Hub MIB Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC describes how a network manager sees the hardware behind an Ethernet port. It also rearranges the definitions so that a new kind of cable or connector can be added without rewriting the whole document.

sections.title: Overview: What a MAU Is
sections.content:
Instances of these object types represent attributes of an IEEE 802.3 MAU. Several types of MAUs are defined in the IEEE 802.3 CSMA/CD standard. These MAUs may be connected to IEEE 802.3 repeaters or to 802.3 (Ethernet-like) interfaces, and for convenience this document calls them "repeater MAUs" and "interface MAUs".

The definitions presented here are based on Section 30.5, "Layer Management for 10 Mb/s, 100 Mb/s, 1000 Mb/s, and 10 Gb/s Medium Attachment Units (MAUs)", Section 30.6, "Management for link Auto-Negotiation", and Annex 30A, "GDMO Specifications for 802.3 managed object classes" of IEEE Std. 802.3-2005. The specification is intended to provide for management of all types of Ethernet/802.3 MAUs.

A MAU can also be "internal", meaning that its functionality is implemented entirely within a device. A managed repeater may contain an internal repeater-MAU or an internal interface-MAU through which management communications originating on one of the repeater's external ports pass, in order to reach the management agent associated with the repeater. Internal MAUs may or may not be managed. If they are managed, objects describing their attributes appear in the dot3RpMauBasicGroup subtree for internal repeater-MAUs and in the dot3IfMauBasicGroup subtree for internal interface-MAUs.
sections.plainLanguage: A MAU is the hardware that sits between the cable and the rest of the network. It can sit behind a repeater port or behind a normal Ethernet interface, and it can also be built into a device rather than bolted on as a separate box.

sections.title: Splitting the MIB into Two Modules
sections.content:
The management definitions provided in this document are intended to be a superset of those defined by RFC 3636.

In order to decrease the need of updating the basic MAU MIB module when a new MAU type, Media Available state, Auto Negotiation capability or Jack type is introduced, all relevant object identities and textual conventions have been moved to a separate, IANA-maintained MIB module called IANA-MAU-MIB. When the IEEE 802.3 working group defines a new MAU type, Media Available state, Auto Negotiation capability or Jack type, only the IANA-maintained module needs to be revised, leaving the basic MAU-MIB unchanged.

The RFC notes that this change is not entirely backward-compatible with MIB modules that currently import MAU type object identity descriptors from the MAU-MIB. Such modules need to be revised to import those descriptors from the IANA-MAU-MIB instead, and management applications that process the object identity definitions, for example to present the DESCRIPTION text to a user, need to get those definitions from the IANA-MAU-MIB. While changes that require such adjustments are not strictly compliant with the SMIv2 rules governing MIB module revisions, the RFC argues that the continued high maintenance cost of not making them justifies the deviation. It adds that the working group was not able to find any example of a MIB module or management application that would actually be negatively affected.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, every new cable type meant a new version of the whole MAU MIB. Now the names live in a separate, small module that IANA can update on its own, so the main module stays as it is.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
It is assumed that an agent implementing MAU-MIB will also implement, at least, the 'system' group defined in the SNMPv2 MIB.

The interface MAU objects specify an extension to the Interfaces MIB. An agent implementing them must also implement the relevant groups of the ifCompliance3 MODULE-COMPLIANCE statement of the Interface MIB, and must fully comply with the dot3Compliance2 MODULE-COMPLIANCE statement of the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB. The value of the object ifMauIfIndex is the same as the value of ifIndex used to instantiate the interface to which the given MAU is connected.

Where the interface MAU objects are used to manage a 10GBASE-W PHY, the agent must also support the Ethernet WAN Interface Sublayer (WIS) MIB and follow the interface layering model specified there. In that case the value of ifMauIfIndex is the value of ifIndex for the layer at the top of the stack. If the interface MAU objects are used to manage a PHY whose MAU type can be changed dynamically, the agent must create ifTable, ifStackTable and ifInvStackTable entries that pertain to the WIS when ifMauDefaultType is changed to a 10GBASE-W variant, and destroy the WIS-related entries when it is changed to a non-10GBASE-W type. Repeater ports are not represented as interfaces in the Interface MIB.

The repeater MAU objects specify an extension to the 802.3 Repeater MIB, and an agent implementing them must also comply with the snmpRptrModCompl compliance statement of that module. The values of rpMauGroupIndex and rpMauPortIndex used to instantiate a repeater MAU variable must be the same as the values of rptrPortGroupIndex and rptrPortIndex used to instantiate the port that the given MAU is connected to.
sections.plainLanguage: These objects do not stand alone. A MAU behind an interface is linked to the interface table, and a MAU behind a repeater is linked to the repeater table, so a manager can find the port a MAU belongs to.

sections.title: Mapping IEEE 802.3 Objects to SNMP Objects
sections.content:
The RFC gives a table mapping the managed objects defined in Clause 30 of IEEE 802.3 to the SNMP objects that carry them. The MAU's identity, aMAUID, maps to rpMauIndex, ifMauIndex or broadMauIndex, depending on whether the MAU sits behind a repeater, behind an interface, or in a broadband context. The MAU type aMAUType maps to rpMauType or ifMauType, the list of possible types aMAUTypeList maps to ifMauTypeListBits, and aMediaAvailable maps to rpMauMediaAvailable or ifMauMediaAvailable.

The count of lost media, aLoseMediaCounter, maps to the media available state exit counters. The jabber flag and counter map to the jabber state and jabbering state enters counters. The administrative state aMAUAdminState, the reset action acResetMAU and the administrative control acMAUAdminControl all map onto the same status object, rpMauStatus or ifMauStatus.

Two groups of IEEE 802.3 objects are left out. The idle error counter aIdleErrorCount is excluded because it is only useful for 100BASE-T2, which is not widely implemented. The three Auto Negotiation selector ability objects are excluded because they are only needed to support isoethernet (802.9a), which MAU-MIB does not support.
sections.plainLanguage: The IEEE standard already defines its own management objects. The RFC shows which SNMP object carries each one, so a manager can translate between the two descriptions.

sections.title: The MAU MIB Objects
sections.content:
The MAU-MIB module defines several tables. The rpMauTable describes MAUs attached to repeater ports and is indexed by the repeater group index, the port index and the MAU index. The ifMauTable describes MAUs attached to interfaces and is indexed by the interface index and the MAU index. The rpJackTable and ifJackTable record the connector type of each managed jack, the ifMauAutoNegTable holds configuration and status for the auto-negotiation function of interface MAUs, and broadMauBasicTable covers broadband MAUs.

Each MAU entry carries a type, a status, a Media Available state, counters for the number of times the link has been lost and the number of times the MAU has entered the jabber state, and a count of false carriers. The status object takes the values other(1), unknown(2), operational(3), standby(4), shutdown(5) and reset(6). It is read-write, so an operator can put a MAU into standby or shut it down, and setting it to reset(6) resets the MAU in the same manner as a power-off, power-on cycle of at least one-half second would.

The MAU type object reports the operational type, which is the result of the auto-negotiation function if that function is enabled or implemented, and otherwise the value of ifMauDefaultType. The ifMauDefaultType object is read-write: it holds the type the MAU reverts to if auto-negotiation is later disabled. The older ifMauTypeList object, which encoded the set of possible types as a sum of powers of two, is deprecated in favour of ifMauTypeListBits, a bit string carrying the same information.

Two notifications are defined. rpMauJabberTrap and ifMauJabberTrap are sent whenever a managed repeater MAU or interface MAU enters the jabber state, and the agent must throttle consecutive traps so that there is at least a five-second gap between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each MAU gets a row of numbers a manager can read: what kind it is, whether it is working, how often the link has dropped and how often it has started transmitting on its own. A few of the values can also be written, to shut a port down or reset it.

sections.title: The IANA-Maintained MAU Module
sections.content:
The IANA-MAU-MIB module defines no management objects. It holds the dot3MauType OBJECT-IDENTITY, one for each standardised MAU type, and four textual conventions that give the enumerated values used by the MAU-MIB: IANAifMauTypeListBits, IANAifMauMediaAvailable, IANAifMauAutoNegCapBits and IANAifJackType. The module lives at mib-2 154, and the base MAU-MIB at mib-2 26.

The type list bits run from bOther(0) to b1000BasePX20U(53), covering 10BASE-T, 100BASE-TX, 1000BASE-X and the 10GBASE family, with the EFM types and 10GBASE-CX4 added since RFC 3636. The Media Available enumeration runs from other(1) to ready(20). The value available(3) means the link, light or loopback is normal, notAvailable(4) means link loss, low light or no loopback, and the remaining values name particular remote faults, such as remoteFault(5), remoteJabber(7) and remoteLinkLoss(8), along with the 10GBASE-W WIS loss of frame and loss of signal values.

Each new MAU type, Media Available state, Auto Negotiation capability or Jack type defined by the IEEE 802.3 working group and approved for publication in a revision of IEEE Std 802.3 is to be added to this module, provided it is suitable for being managed by the base objects in the MAU-MIB. An Expert Review, as defined in RFC 2434, is required for each modification. Where a new MAU type requires additional managed objects, or has side effects on the behaviour of existing managed objects, a standards-track specification is also required.
sections.plainLanguage: The IANA module is the list of names: one per cable type, one per fault reason, one per connector shape. IANA adds to it when IEEE standardises something new, and the RFC requires an expert review of each addition.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IANA-MAU-MIB defines no management objects, so the RFC says meaningful security considerations can only be written for MIB modules that define management objects.

There are a number of management objects in the MAU-MIB that have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write. Setting them can have a serious effect on the operation of the network, including enabling or disabling a MAU, changing a MAU's default type, enabling, disabling or restarting auto-negotiation, and modifying the capabilities that a MAU advertises during auto-negotiation. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and the support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive or vulnerable. In some environments it may be undesirable to allow unauthorised parties to access statistics or status information about individual links in a network. It is thus important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is no control over who on the secure network may read or change the objects in the MAU-MIB module. The RFC recommends that implementors use the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is not recommended. It then places the responsibility on the operator to configure the SNMP entity so that the objects are reachable only by principals with legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these values can switch a port off or change what it advertises, so writing to them can break a network. The RFC says to use the encrypted and authenticated version of SNMP, SNMPv3, and to keep the objects away from people who have no business reading them.
